rows.description: A teacher notices one child joining the football group while the other stays with the art crowd. Neither did anything wrong; time and new activities pull them into different circles.
The one left behind feels a dull ache and wonders what he did. Children rarely explain a drift, so the hurt one may assume rejection when the real cause is only busier days and new company.
A parent helps the child say hello, invite the old friend to one game, and accept that friends can be different for different seasons. Loss is real, but it does not mean the friendship was false.

A student is drawn to a classmate's humour and confidence and imagines a future from a few conversations. Infatuation fills in the blanks generously, so the person seen is partly the person wished for.
He replies to her stories, suggests coffee and reads her texts many times. Under the play is fear of rejection, and small signals such as reply speed feel enormously important.

rows.subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]
rows.description: As they meet more they see habits, moods and differences in values. The glow fades a little, and the important question shifts from "do I like how this feels?" to "do I like who this is?".
One says "I would like us to be exclusive. Where do you stand?" Asking directly risks a no but ends weeks of guessing, and the answer, whichever it is, lets each act on facts.

A friend notices them adjusting to each other's friends, food and family expectations. In many Indian families the question of caste, religion or a future household appears early and tests whether the couple can face the outside together.
They commit after seeing each other in stress as well as in joy, and speak honestly about goals. Commitment is a decision made with open eyes, not a feeling that simply arrives.

With the deadline near, fear finally gives energy and the assignment is done overnight. It often works well enough to teach the wrong lesson that delaying is fine, while the cost of stress and quality is ignored.
After the deadline, the person calls themself lazy and vows to change, then repeats the pattern. Harsh self-talk adds the very discomfort that makes the next task feel harder to face.
A student sets a short timer, works in a library or with a friend, and writes just a messy first paragraph. Lowering the bar for starting removes the dread, and momentum usually does the rest.

rows.subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
rows.subtype: Stage 1: The news and the glow [Actor]
rows.description: A well-liked engineer is made team lead and feels proud and validated after years of effort. Family and friends congratulate, and the rise in status feels like a reward earned.

rows.subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
rows.description: The new lead starts to see themself as the smart one, quotes their own past decisions and enjoys deference. Praise slowly turns into an expectation of it.

rows.subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
rows.description: The lead skips lunches with old friends, talks down to them and shares less. Some distance is natural in a new role, but a sense of being above them is not.

rows.subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
rows.description: Critical remarks are brushed off as jealousy or lack of vision. The ego protects a new identity by treating any challenge as a threat, and the leader stops learning.

rows.subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
rows.description: A poor call made without consulting others costs the team a delay. Blame is first pushed onto the team, and the leader feels shaken as the halo cracks.

rows.subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
rows.description: The lead owns the error openly, thanks those who warned them and asks for candid feedback. Acknowledging fault in public tends to raise respect rather than lower it.
